title: JSON Merge Patch
summary: This specification defines the JSON merge patch format and processing rules, primarily for use with the HTTP PATCH method to describe changes to a target resource's content. It replaces RFC 7386.

plainLanguage.summary:
Merge patch is a way of saying what to change in a JSON document by sending a JSON document that looks like the part you want changed. A field you include is set to the value you send. A field set to null is removed.

Everything the patch does not mention is left alone, so a client sends only the part it cares about. The catch is that arrays are replaced as a whole, so you cannot change one element of a list with this format.

questions: remove a field with merge patch
how to remove a field with merge patch
subtitle: Describe a change to a JSON document by sending a small document that looks like the part you want changed.

tldr.problem: HTTP PATCH needs a format for saying what to change in a resource, and the earlier JSON patch format needed a list of instructions such as add, replace and remove, each one naming a path into the document.
tldr.mechanism: JSON merge patch replaces that with a small JSON document that looks like the part of the target you want to change. Members in the patch are added or replaced, and a null value asks for a member to be removed. The RFC defines the format, the exact processing rules and the application/merge-patch+json media type.
tldr.outcome: A client can express most edits as a copy of the target with the changes marked in place, and the server works out the operations by comparing the two. The RFC obsoletes RFC 7386.

today: RFC 7396 is a Proposed Standard from October 2014. It obsoletes RFC 7386 and has not itself been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
This specification defines the JSON merge patch document format, the processing rules and the associated MIME media type identifier. The merge patch format is primarily intended for use with the HTTP PATCH method as a means of describing a set of modifications to a target resource's content.

A JSON merge patch document describes changes to be made to a target JSON document using a syntax that closely mimics the document being modified. Recipients of a merge patch document determine the exact set of changes being requested by comparing the content of the provided patch against the current content of the target document. If the provided merge patch contains members that do not appear within the target, those members are added. If the target does contain the member, the value is replaced. Null values in the merge patch are given special meaning to indicate the removal of existing values in the target.

The design means that merge patch documents are suitable for describing modifications to JSON documents that primarily use objects for their structure and do not make use of explicit null values. The merge patch format is not appropriate for all JSON syntaxes.
sections.plainLanguage: The idea is that the patch looks like the target. You send the part you want to change, copied, with your changes marked in it, and the server works out what you meant.

sections.title: The MergePatch Function
sections.content:
Recipients of merge patch documents are responsible for comparing the merge patch with the current content of the target resource to determine the specific set of change operations to be applied. The RFC gives the whole procedure as a function in pseudocode, taking the target resource document and the merge patch document as arguments. The target argument can be any JSON value or undefined; the patch argument can be any JSON value.

There are a few things to note about the function. If the patch is anything other than an object, the result will always be to replace the entire target with the entire patch. Also, it is not possible to patch part of a target that is not an object, such as to replace just some of the values in an array.

The operation is defined to operate at the level of data items, not at the level of textual representation. There is no expectation that it will preserve features at the textual level such as white space, member ordering, and number precision beyond what is available in the target's implementation. Even if the target implementation allows multiple name and value pairs with the same name, the result of the operation on such objects is not defined.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules are short: objects are merged member by member, a null deletes a member, and anything that is not an object replaces the target outright.

sections.title: A Worked Example
sections.content:
Given a target document with a title, an author object holding a given name and a family name, a tags array and a content string, a user agent wishing to change the value of the title, add a new phoneNumber member, remove the familyName member from the author object, and replace the tags array so that it does not include the word sample would send a PATCH request whose body is {"title": "Hello!", "phoneNumber": "+01-123-456-7890", "author": {"familyName": null}, "tags": [ "example" ]}.

Applying the patch leaves the title changed, the phone number added, the family name gone, the given name still there because the patch never mentioned it, the tags array replaced by its single remaining element, and the content string untouched.
sections.plainLanguage: Notice what the patch does not contain. The given name and the content string are not in the patch, and both survive the change. Only the names that appear are touched.

sections.title: The Media Type Registration
sections.content:
The specification registers the MIME media type application/merge-patch+json, with no required parameters and no optional parameters. Resources that use the media type are required to conform to the application/json media type and are therefore subject to the same encoding considerations.

The registration records that the security considerations are as defined in the specification itself, that the intended usage is COMMON, that there are no restrictions on usage, that no applications using this media type are currently known, that the magic number and file extension are not applicable and that the Macintosh file type code is TEXT.
sections.plainLanguage: The body of a merge patch request is ordinary JSON, with a content type that says which kind of JSON it is: a patch rather than a whole document.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The media type allows user agents to indicate their intention for the server to determine the specific set of change operations to be applied to a target resource. It is therefore the server's responsibility to determine the appropriateness of any given change as well as the user agent's authorization to request such changes. How such determinations are made is out of the scope of this specification.

All of the security considerations discussed for the HTTP PATCH method apply to all uses of that method with the application/merge-patch+json media type.
sections.plainLanguage: The patch only says what the client would like changed. Whether the client is allowed to make that change, and whether the change makes sense, is the server's job.

sections.title: Example Test Cases
sections.content:
The RFC gives a table of original documents, patches and results, which serves as a set of test cases. Replacing a value gives the new value. Adding a member that was absent adds it. A null value removes the member, and a null value for a member that is absent leaves the document alone. Replacing an array with a string, or a string with an array, replaces the whole value. A nested object is merged member by member, so a null inside it removes that inner member only.

Some of the cases show the limits. A patch that is an array replaces the entire target with that array. A patch of null makes the result null, and a patch of a plain string makes the result that string, even when the target was an object. An empty object patched with a nested object whose leaves are null yields an empty object at the end, because the leaves were never there to remove.
sections.plainLanguage: These cases are the practical rules. Read them as a checklist: an object merges, a null deletes, anything else replaces everything.

items.title: Object patch, object target
items.text: Merge the members one by one, recursing into nested objects.

items.title: Object patch, other target
items.text: The target is treated as an empty object and the patch is merged into it.

items.title: Null value
items.text: The member is removed from the target, if it is there.

items.title: Non-object patch
items.text: The whole target is replaced by the patch.

items.title: Arrays
items.text: An array is replaced as a whole; it cannot be patched part by part.

items.title: Unmentioned members
items.text: They are left exactly as they were in the target.
